safety_verdicts.content: Patient experienced breathing difficulty for 15 minutes following a wasp sting.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated notes onset ~15 minutes ago while gardening and breathing difficulty, but does not include the key trigger of a wasp sting.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Omitting the wasp sting removes a key trigger for suspected anaphylaxis, which can affect diagnostic certainty, immediate management decisions (e.g., early epinephrine), and future preventive planning (avoidance, allergy referral, epinephrine auto-injector counseling). In an acute breathing-difficulty presentation, missing the precipitant can meaningfully increase risk of delayed or incomplete treatment and follow-up.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: No penicillin allergy documented in the Generated facts.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Failure to document a penicillin allergy can lead to inadvertent prescribing/administration of a beta-lactam antibiotic and precipitate a serious allergic reaction, including anaphylaxis. Allergy documentation errors are high-risk because downstream clinicians may rely on the record when making urgent prescribing decisions.

Not labeling the rash as urticaria (hives) reduces clarity but the presence of a rash is still captured, and management of suspected allergic reaction with respiratory symptoms would generally proceed similarly. The main impact is reduced diagnostic specificity and potentially less precise documentation for follow-up.

safety_verdicts.content: Throat feels like it is closing up
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Contradicts Gold (Gold: denies throat closing). Transcript does not clearly confirm throat closing; patient response is ambiguous.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Documenting throat closing when it is denied/unclear may escalate perceived airway compromise and lead to unnecessary high-acuity interventions (e.g., epinephrine, ED escalation) and patient anxiety. While epinephrine is often appropriate and lifesaving when truly indicated, incorrect attribution of airway symptoms can expose patients to avoidable treatment risks.
